title: Nonlinear Functions
intro: Not every function is a straight line. This chapter covers the main nonlinear families on the SAT — quadratic, exponential and polynomial functions — focusing on evaluating them and recognising their behavior. Read each topic, work the problems with the hint ladder, then take the 8-question topic test.

items.name: Polynomial

topics.name: Quadratic Functions
topics.details: A quadratic function has the form f(x) = ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0, and its graph is a parabola. Evaluating one means substituting the input and applying the exponent before multiplying — for f(x) = 2x² − 3x + 1, f(2) = 2(4) − 3(2) + 1 = 3. Watch signs when the input is negative, since squaring makes it positive. The sign of a tells you the parabola opens up (a > 0) or down (a < 0). Quadratics appear throughout SAT Advanced Math; here the focus is careful evaluation, using parentheses around the input to avoid sign and order-of-operations errors.

topics.name: Exponential Functions
topics.details: An exponential function has the form f(x) = a · bˣ, where the variable is in the exponent. The base b controls behavior: b > 1 gives growth (values rise quickly), and 0 < b < 1 gives decay (values shrink toward zero). To evaluate, raise the base to the input power first, then multiply by a — for f(x) = 3 · 2ˣ, f(4) = 3 · 2⁴ = 3 · 16 = 48. Note f(0) = a, since b⁰ = 1. Exponential functions grow far faster than linear or quadratic ones for large x. The SAT tests evaluating them and identifying growth versus decay from the base.

solved.problem: Does y = 100 · (1.2)ˣ show growth or decay?
Does y = 80 · (0.5)ˣ show growth or decay?

unsolved.problem: Does y = 50 · (3)ˣ represent growth or decay?
Does y = 200 · (0.8)ˣ represent growth or decay?

topics.name: Polynomial Functions
topics.details: A polynomial function is a sum of terms of the form (coefficient)·xⁿ with whole-number exponents, such as f(x) = 2x³ − 4x + 1. The degree is the highest power of x, and it shapes the graph’s overall behavior and how many turns or roots it can have. Linear (degree 1) and quadratic (degree 2) are the simplest polynomials; cubics are degree 3. To evaluate, substitute and apply each power carefully, watching signs when the input is negative — for f(x) = x³ + 2, f(−2) = (−2)³ + 2 = −8 + 2 = −6. The SAT tests reading the degree and evaluating low-degree polynomials accurately.

solved.problem: What is the degree of f(x) = 2x³ + 5x − 1?
What is the degree of f(x) = x⁴ + 3x² + 7?

unsolved.problem: What is the degree of f(x) = 5x³ + 2x − 8?
What is the degree of f(x) = 3x⁵ + x² − 4?
